descs.t: President Trump has gone after Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, saying Sharia law is never coming to America, as Republican Mike Rogers campaigns hard in Wayne County near Detroit. Voters in Detroit are split on camera. We walk through the final stretch of the Michigan Senate contest and what each side is betting on.

The Michigan Senate race between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers is coming down to Wayne County, and Trump has made Sharia law part of the fight. Add a hidden camera clip of Rashida Tlaib defending El-Sayed and Dana Perino's challenge on what Jewish voters are being told. We break down the pressure points that could decide the seat.

Trump told Abdul El-Sayed that Sharia law is never coming to America, and Michigan's Senate race just turned into a referendum on the left's embrace of Islamist politics. Mike Rogers is storming Detroit, Black voters are talking back on live TV, and Jewish voters are being lectured about a moral obligation. We show why this race matters far beyond Michigan.

intro.plain: Michigan's Senate race is in its final stretch. Trump has gone after Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, saying Sharia law is never coming to America, and Republican Mike Rogers is campaigning in Wayne County near Detroit. Voters there are split on camera. Let's go through where this race stands. Chat, who do you think takes Michigan?
intro.mid: Michigan could come down to Wayne County. Mike Rogers is campaigning hard near Detroit, Trump is hammering Abdul El-Sayed on Sharia law, and Rashida Tlaib is caught on hidden camera defending him. Let's look at what could actually swing this seat. Chat, does the Sharia attack help Rogers or backfire?
intro.bold: Trump just told Abdul El-Sayed, Sharia law is never coming to America. And in Michigan, the Democrats' coalition is showing cracks: Black voters pushing back on live TV, Jewish voters told they have a moral obligation. Mike Rogers is storming Detroit. Chat, is Michigan about to send a message to the whole country?

hook.plain: Trump says Sharia law is never coming to America, and he said it about Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate. Here is where the race stands.
hook.mid: Michigan's Senate seat could come down to one county near Detroit. Here are the pressure points that will decide it.
hook.bold: Trump told Abdul El-Sayed to screw off with Sharia law. Now Michigan's Senate race is a test of the left's coalition. Watch it crack.

descs.t: The Pentagon estimates the US war with Iran has cost more than $47 billion, $47.1 billion according to the figure given to Congress, eight months into the fight. Reports also say the US has warned Gulf allies about new strikes. We walk through the estimate and what it covers.

The Iran war has now cost the US over $47 billion, according to a Pentagon estimate reported by Reuters, as reports say Washington has warned Gulf allies about new strikes. Meanwhile the UN nuclear chief says Iran has not tried to repair the nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes. We weigh the cost against what the campaign has done to the regime.

Eight months and over $47 billion into the war with Iran's regime, reports say Trump is preparing a short, intense war after Election Day and Gulf states have been warned to brace. The UN nuclear chief says Iran has not repaired its damaged nuclear sites. We break down the cost, the pressure and what comes after the midterms.

intro.plain: The Pentagon has told Congress the Iran war has cost the US 47.1 billion dollars, eight months in. At the same time, reports say the US has warned Gulf allies about new strikes. I want to go through what that number means and where this goes next. Question for the chat: is that price worth it to you?
intro.mid: Over 47 billion dollars. That is the Pentagon's estimate for the Iran war so far. And it may not be over: reports say Gulf allies have been warned about new strikes, while the UN nuclear chief says Iran has not repaired its damaged nuclear sites. So the chat question is simple: is this money well spent?
intro.bold: Eight months and over 47 billion dollars into the war with the Islamic Republic, and reports say Trump is preparing a short, intense war after Election Day. Gulf states have been told to brace. Iran's damaged nuclear sites still are not repaired. The regime is still standing. Chat, tell me: should America finish the job?

hook.plain: The Pentagon says the Iran war has cost the US $47.1 billion so far. Here is what that estimate says, and what reports say comes next.
hook.mid: Over $47 billion spent, Gulf allies warned about new strikes, and Iran's damaged nuclear sites still unrepaired. Here is what the money has bought, and what it has not.
hook.bold: $47 billion in, and reports say a short, intense war could come right after Election Day. Here is what that bill means for finishing off the regime.

descs.t: Flavio Bolsonaro and his family will receive US visas after he left Brazil, the State Department says. He lost Sunday's presidential election to Lula da Silva, and a Supreme Court order told him to hand over his passports, which were then cancelled. We walk through how he left, what Washington said and what Brazil's courts are investigating.

Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil for the United States after losing to Lula, and the State Department says he and his family will get visas. Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered his passports surrendered and opened an investigation into alleged foreign funding, while Trump said he would approve his coming. We look at what each side claims and what it means for the US and Brazil.

Flavio Bolsonaro, who reportedly won nearly 60 million votes, defied a passport order from Justice Alexandre de Moraes and left Brazil, and Washington is giving his family visas. His allies call it political persecution by the Lula government, while Brazil's courts point to investigations. We lay out the passport order, the investigations and why the US stepped in.

intro.plain: Big one out of Brazil. Flavio Bolsonaro lost Sunday's presidential election to Lula, a Supreme Court justice ordered him to hand over his passports, he did not, and now he is out of the country. The State Department says he and his family will get US visas. So, chat: should Washington be taking in Brazil's defeated candidate, yes or no?
intro.mid: Flavio Bolsonaro is out of Brazil. Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered his passports surrendered, they were cancelled when he did not, and the State Department now says he and his family get US visas. Trump says he approves and calls the election really strange. Brazil's court is investigating alleged foreign funding. Chat, is this justice in Brazil or a crackdown on the opposition?
intro.bold: Lula wins, and within days his main rival is out of the country. Flavio Bolsonaro's allies say an order to keep him in Brazil came seven minutes after Lula was declared the winner. He refused to hand over his passports, he left, and Washington is giving his family visas. Trump says he would approve. Chat, is Brazil now punishing people for running against Lula?

hook.plain: Flavio Bolsonaro lost to Lula, was told to surrender his passports, and left Brazil anyway. Now the State Department says his family gets US visas. Here is how it happened.
hook.mid: A court order, cancelled passports and a flight out: Flavio Bolsonaro is gone, and the US is giving him visas. Here is what each side says and what it means for Washington and Brazil.
hook.bold: Days after Lula won, his rival's passports were cancelled. Flavio Bolsonaro left anyway, and America is opening the door. This is how Brazil's opposition leader ended up in exile.

descs.t: Netanyahu's bloc is slightly ahead in Israel's election but short of the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority, with about 70% of votes counted. Counts put his bloc at 54 seats to 49 for Gadi Eisenkot's bloc, with Arab parties at 17. We walk through the count, the turnout and the paths to a government.

Benjamin Netanyahu says his bloc has a decisive majority, while Gadi Eisenkot says Israelis voted for change. The BBC reports Netanyahu's bloc slightly ahead but short of a majority with 70% counted, after the election commission rejected Likud's request to extend voting hours. We look at what the numbers show and who could form the next government.

Netanyahu defied the polls again: Likud is set to be Israel's largest party and his bloc leads the count, but 61 seats are still out of reach. Turnout hit 74.3%, Arab parties hold 17 seats, and Eisenkot claims a victory for change. We break down what this means for Israel and for who governs next.

intro.plain: Israel voted, and with about 70 percent counted, Netanyahu's bloc is slightly ahead but short of the 61 seats needed for a majority. Counts have his bloc at 54 and Eisenkot's at 49, with Arab parties at 17. Turnout hit 74.3 percent. So my question for you in the chat: do you think Netanyahu forms the next government?
intro.mid: Netanyahu says his bloc has a decisive majority. Eisenkot says Israelis voted for change. The count says neither has 61 seats yet, with Netanyahu's bloc at 54 and Eisenkot's at 49. Arab parties sit at 17 and could decide this. Tell me in the chat: who do you think ends up as prime minister?
intro.bold: Netanyahu defied the polls again. Likud looks set to be the largest party and his bloc is leading the count, while people online were already celebrating his defeat. But he is still short of 61 seats, and this is not over. For Israel's security, this result matters. Chat, tell me: is this a win for Israel, or not yet?

hook.plain: Netanyahu's bloc leads Israel's count, 54 seats to 49, but the line for a majority is 61. Here is where the votes stand and who could still form a government.
hook.mid: Netanyahu claims a decisive majority. Eisenkot claims a victory for change. Both cannot be right. Here is what the count actually shows, and why Arab parties could decide it.
hook.bold: They celebrated his defeat on election night. Then the count came in, and Netanyahu was ahead again. But he is still short of 61 seats. Here is what decides it.

descs.t: The Texas Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico enters its final days, with early voting ending Friday, October 30. Trump rallied in Lubbock for Paxton while Talarico held rallies in Midland and Lubbock. We walk through what each camp is saying and what the early vote does and does not tell us.

Ken Paxton and James Talarico are fighting for a Texas Senate seat that could matter for control of the chamber. Trump told Texans he needs Paxton in the Senate, while some Republican voters say on camera they will vote Talarico. We look at the early vote claims from both sides and Talarico's legislative record.

Texas chooses between Ken Paxton and James Talarico, and both camps say the state's way of life is on the ballot. Trump went after Talarico's platform on guns, oil and children, while one Texas Republican warned his side is getting beat in the early vote. We break down the record, the rallies and the turnout fight.

intro.plain: Texas early voting ends Friday, and the Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico is getting loud. Trump rallied for Paxton in Lubbock, Talarico held his own rallies in Midland and Lubbock, and both sides are claiming the early vote. This seat could matter for the whole Senate. So tell me in the chat: are you in Texas, and have you voted yet?
intro.mid: Some Texas Republicans are now saying on camera they will vote for James Talarico, while one Republican warns his side is getting beat in the early vote. Trump says he needs Ken Paxton in the Senate. Early voting ends Friday, and this seat could shape control of the Senate. Chat, tell me: is Texas really in play, or is this hype?
intro.bold: Trump went straight at James Talarico in Lubbock, guns, oil, kids, all of it, and Ken Paxton says Texas is choosing its way of life. On the other side, Talarico is packing rooms and some Republicans say they are crossing over. Early voting ends Friday. Chat, be honest: what decides this race, Talarico's record or turnout?

hook.plain: Early voting in Texas ends Friday, and the Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico is closer to the wire than anyone expected. Here is what each side is claiming.
hook.mid: A Texas Republican says his side is getting beat in the early vote. Trump says he needs Paxton. Here is what is actually going on in this race.
hook.bold: Trump called James Talarico's platform insane, and Ken Paxton says Texas itself is on the ballot. Six days out, here is the fight in full.

descs.t: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has signed the order expelling a Cuban diplomat accused of shoving an American staffer during a clash with UN Ambassador Mike Waltz. The confrontation broke out during the UN debate on the US embargo of Cuba, as Waltz called out the wealth of the Castro regime's families. We walk through what happened at the podium, who the diplomat is, and why he is now on a flight back to Cuba.

Mike Waltz told Cuba's delegation at the UN that this is not Havana, and days later the diplomat accused of getting physical with a US staffer is being sent home on Marco Rubio's order. The clash came as the UN again voted against the US embargo, though nearly triple the usual number of countries voted no, abstained or sat out. We break down the clash, the expulsion and what both say about Washington's new line on Havana.

Cuba's regime sent its diplomats to the UN to shout down America's ambassador, and one of them is now accused of shoving an American. Marco Rubio signed his expulsion and Mike Waltz used the moment to put Havana's corruption and its 800 political prisoners in front of the world. We show the confrontation, the fallout, and why intimidation tactics that work in Havana failed in New York.

intro.plain: Big story out of the UN. During the debate on the Cuba embargo, Cuba's delegation confronted Ambassador Mike Waltz at the podium, and a Cuban official is accused of shoving an American staffer. Now Marco Rubio has signed the order to expel him, and he's on a flight back to Cuba. Chat, was expulsion the right call, or should Washington have gone further?
intro.mid: Mike Waltz told Cuba's delegation, this isn't Havana, you are not going to intimidate me. Now one of their diplomats, accused of shoving an American staffer, is being sent home on Marco Rubio's order. And the same day, far more countries than usual refused to back Cuba's embargo resolution. Chat, is Havana losing its grip on the UN crowd it used to count on?
intro.bold: Cuba's regime thought it could push an American diplomat around at the UN. Wrong country. A Cuban official accused of shoving a US staffer is now on a one way flight home, signed off by Marco Rubio, while Mike Waltz kept talking about the regime's corruption and its 800 political prisoners. Chat, which regime should get this treatment next?

hook.plain: A Cuban official is accused of shoving an American staffer at the UN. Now Marco Rubio has signed his expulsion. Here is exactly how it happened.
hook.mid: This isn't Havana. That is what Mike Waltz told Cuba's delegation, and now one of its diplomats is being sent home. Here is why it matters.
hook.bold: Cuba's regime tried to bully an American ambassador at the UN, and one of its diplomats is now on a one way flight home. Watch how it backfired.

descs.t: A United Nations commission says Israel continues what it calls genocidal acts in Gaza despite the ceasefire, a claim carried by outlets including CBS News and Arab News. The report lands as Israel holds an election and Gaza residents watch the results. We go through what the commission claims, what it rests on, and how Israel and its critics are responding.

A UN commission is accusing Israel of genocidal acts in Gaza even after the ceasefire, and the word genocide is back in parliaments and on social media. At the same time, Arab parties are voting in Israel's election. We test the commission's claim against what is on the record, and ask why the UN keeps reaching for the heaviest word in international law.

The UN says Israel is committing genocidal acts in Gaza, after a ceasefire, during an election in which Arab citizens of Israel cast their votes. We take the commission's claim apart, look at who keeps pushing the genocide label and why, and show what this campaign means for Israel and for the region.

intro.plain: A UN commission now says Israel continues what it calls genocidal acts in Gaza, even after the ceasefire. CBS News and others are carrying it, and it lands right as Israel holds an election. I want to go through what the commission is actually claiming and what it rests on. Chat, do you think reports like this still move public opinion?
intro.mid: There's a ceasefire in Gaza, and the UN commission still says genocidal acts. That word is doing a lot of work, and it's showing up everywhere. Meanwhile Arab parties are voting in Israel's election. Let's test the claim against the record. Chat, what would it take for you to call something genocide?
intro.bold: The UN is at it again. A commission says Israel continues genocidal acts in Gaza, after a ceasefire, while Arab citizens of Israel vote in a free election. That's the country they call genocidal. We're going to take this claim apart piece by piece. Chat, why do you think the UN keeps reaching for this word?

hook.plain: A UN commission says Israel continues genocidal acts in Gaza, despite the ceasefire. Here is what the claim says and what it leaves out.
hook.mid: A ceasefire is in place, and the UN still says genocide. Let's test that claim against the record, one piece at a time.
hook.bold: Arab citizens of Israel just voted in a free election, and the UN calls the country genocidal. Watch how this claim falls apart.
